messages.subject_clean: occupancy estimates with uninformative CI
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Quick thoughts:

 Just generally, sounds like maybe you want to be thinking about ranef (the estimate of the occupancy state of these particular islands at these times) rather than predict. There may or may not a big difference.
Small data/boundary issues: one thing might be to consider a penalized likelihood approach (occuPen). Alternatively, it seems as though you might be aggregating a lot of information into your observation matrix (are the dimensions 10 x 2?). Depends what you want to do and whether the sampling design is appropriate, but it seems to me that you could consider a transect as a site (rather than an island), and you might think about bird abundance in relation to the distribution of rats across islands (i.e., the proportion an island occupied rather than whether the island has any rats at all): this would at least give you more d.f. to work with.
Cheers,

John

Thanks for your input, John - much appreciated.  I'll look into ranef and occuPen.  As per your suggestions in #2...  I understand considering each transect as a site, as opposed to each island.  However, I'm not certain about looking at the distribution of rats across islands themselves.  For all islands, the placement of my transects was based on accessible habitat - littoral strand forest zones.  The Rock Islands of Palau are characterised by shear limestone faces that generally rise abruptly from the water, most of which are undercut at the water's edge.  However, a handful also support fringing or skirting areas of sandy littoral beach strand habitat.  These islands / beach strand areas specifically are those used for tourist operations (basically picnic areas for divers) and such habitat is overwhelmingly preferred by megapodes for breeding.  Their preference by both tourists and megapodes is a good part of the reason I targeted these areas for surveys, the other being their accessibility.  On some islands, these areas make up only a relatively small percentage of total land area.   Thus, I can see how one could look at the distribution of rats across these beach strand areas but not so much across entire islands themselves.  My sampling design isn't really set in a way to appropriately accommodate this, as far as I can see it.

Secondly, I'm not really focussing on whether these islands have rats (they all do, something I knew prior to beginning my surveys) but whether their numbers are correlated with those of megpapodes and also correlated with tourist presence.

Paul

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] RN model to estimate abundance per site
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lain,

before I get into the issue of camera traps and estimating abundance, here a few points:

backTransform (and predict with "state") give you the mean abundance based on the covariates in the model. Since you have no occupancy covariates the estimates will be the same for all of your sites. ranef() gives site-specific estimates using the data AND the parameter estimates (which in your case assumes no difference across all sites). Now I am not quite sure why you are interested in site specific estimates but not in the effect of covariates on the abundance (e.g. habitat type). It would not make much sense to compare those estimates in a second step for the two habitats, in that case you should model the covariates directly in the occupancy model.

Now there is a larger issue with estimating "abundance" using a RN occupancy model and camera traps. Camera traps are point samples that are not associated with a specific area. There is therefore no way to translate these "abundance" values into density values and not even a clear way to interpret them. Let's assume that you get abundance estimates of 2 for jaguar and 2 for tapir for a specific station. That would mean that the camera is included in the home range of 2 jaguars and 2 tapirs. Now jaguars have home ranges of several 100 km2 while tapirs have home ranges of maybe 2-5 km2 so even though you get the same "abundance" estimates the densities of the two species are hugely different. This means that there is no way to compare abundance estimates across species.

Things get even more complicated when you consider animal movement. Assume you place tow cameras in an animals home range. One close to the home range center (where the animal spends a lot of time) and one closer to the home range edge (where the animal spends less time). The camera in the home range center would get a much larger number of images than the camera at the edge and the RN model would interpreter that as a higher "abundance" even though there is just one animal in both cameras. We have observed this regularly with species such as agouti, paca or deer.

I personally think that the RN model is useful with camera trap data exactly because it improves occupancy estimates when there is the kind of heterogeneity just described that can not be modeled with covariates. You could probably (with some caution) also interpret "abundance" as intensity of habitat use when comparing different habitat types or other covariates, but you can again not compare across species. Occupancy models are a useful tool exactly when you have covariates you want to model but they give you little information in the absence of covariates.

If you want to estimate true abundance you might want to take a look at a recent paper by Howe.

Howe, E. J., Buckland, S. T., Després-Einspenner, M.-L. and Kühl, H. S. (2017), Distance sampling with camera traps. Methods Ecol Evol. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12790

Best,

Mathias

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mathias,

Thank you very much for your feedback, I agree with you. And yes, there was no covariate for sites in this model, so estimates would be the same! (that was a silly question, sorry). I understand your point that there is no much sense not to use covariates along with the estimations of abundance/occ. To examine the effect of the covariates on mammalian community composition, I used the mvabund  R package(see Warton et al 2015 and Wang et al 2016). I actually have my analysis done. However, I have received a recommendation to explore alternatives accounting for detection probabilities, so I´m exploring these. The mvabund approach has the advantage that you can analyze all the covariates and all the species simultaneously, so you don´t have to do this one by one (and is better than common multivariate approaches). I will try to use the covariates within this approach in unmarked anyways and compare. Thanks.

My research design was thought for richness and occupancy estimation of the assemblage, not for density or true abundance for a particular species, strictly speaking. However, it is always good to analyze some kind “relative abundance” (composition, frequency, intensity of hab use) along with the richness... But, I was not interested in true abundances/densities, and therefore my design is not suitable for this (at least not for all the species). It seems that the fact that some species abundance estimations, using ranef(), have large CI (with or without covariates) could be a good argument to probably keep my analysis as it is (using independent pictures and frequencies), but further thoughts would be great to consider. I´ll keep exploring this occRN framework and compare with my previous analysis.

Just a final question, it seems that this occRN model is not good for common species, is this a general recommendation?

Thanks much again for these useful observations.

Best

Lain

messages.body_plain:
Dear Gabrielle,

 I believe the data set is sufficiently small that it is challenging to properly estimate all of the model parameters, especially with the NB model, and with such low detection probabilities. This issue is addressed in some detail by these two papers here which you'll have to read through and try to understand.
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12246/full
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12521/full
As a consequence I think you should probably rule out the NB model for this data set and default to the ZIP and Poisson models.
(also see the Kery and Royle book , Applied Hierarchical Modeling, chapter 6).
 Marc Kery has a relevant paper in review which I wonder if he'll provide on this email list?

 In reply to your specific question about whether this indicates a lack of effect of the covariate or a lack of power due to small sample size, this is not a question that can be answered definitively. You can do a power analysis to give you some ideas about power and sample size requirements which I highly recommend!

 Power to detect abundance effects is definitely affected strongly by the number of sites but also very important is the repeatability of counts: low detection (low repeatability of counts) leads to very low power to detect effects I think.

regards,
andy

In this case your data just barely obtains a unique maximum likelihood estimate.  ("barely obtains" is a term I just made up.)  One can see this with the large standard errors you see for lambda and p.  Also the estimated correlation between the estimators of lambda and p is nearly -1.0 which is not a good sign (estimate is -0.9997579).  In addition, the contour plot of the log likelihood surface indicates both the high correlation and large standard errors.  I know such data is expensive to collect but in this case it just isn't enough to obtain estimates of probably anyone's desired precision.

Here is some R code to find the correlation and produce the contour plot.

  mNull <- pcount(~1 ~1, data= UMF, K=10000, control=list(reltol=0.0000000001))  #or K=100
  lambda.hat = backTransform(mNull, type="state")
  p.hat = backTransform(mNull, type="det")

# Find correlation of the estimators of lambda and p
  covmat = solve(mNull@opt$hessian)
  covmat[1,2]/(covmat[1,1]*covmat[2,2])^0.5

# Contour plot of log likelihood surface
  p = 0.01 + (0.1-0.01)*c(0:250)/250
  lambda = 1 + (40-1)*c(0:250)/250
  logL = function(lambda,p) {
    -(-57*lambda*p + 57*lambda*p^2 - 19*lambda*p^3 - 3*log(2) - log(4) +
    18*log(lambda) + 5*log(1 + lambda*(1 - p)^3) + log(2 + lambda*(1 - p)^3) +
    log(2 - lambda*(-4 - lambda*(1 - p)^3)*(1 - p)^3) +
    log(1 - lambda*(-3 - lambda*(1 - p)^3)*(1 - p)^3) + 26*log(1 - p) + 28*log(p))
  }
  z = outer(lambda,p,logL)
                                                                        library(devEMF)
  emf("c:\\users\\jim nelia\\Desktop\\logL contours.emf")
  contour(lambda,p,z,las=1,xlab="lambda",ylab="p",main="Log likelihood",
    levels=c(51.4,52,60,70,80,90))

# Add in the location of the maximum likelihood estimates
  points(lambda.hat@estimate,p.hat@estimate,pch=16,col="red")
  dev.off()

For counts that are small and where there are no continuous covariates the log likelihood can be written explicitly and relatively compactly (i.e., no need for approximating a sum).  I've also attached a figure showing the contour plot.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All-

Although this is my first post to the group, I find myself searching through the archives on a regular basis. Thank you to everyone who contributes to this group!

I have hit a  sticky spot in my analyses and am seeking some advice to get out. I am using the gdistsamp model to estimate densities among surveyed populations and calculate derived population estimates. The problem I am having is with using the parboot function to estimate confidence intervals for the derived parameters.

My best fit model uses a negative binomial distribution and includes an effect of year (1-4) and population (A-F) on lambda (the rest are constant).

Using vignettes, namely Chandler (2017) distsamp, and the supplemental information from Sillett et al. (2012), I built the following script:

# Assemble empty data frames to populate using predict()
> year<-rep(1:4, length=24)
> pop<-rep(c("A","B","C","D","E","F"), each=4)
> nd<-cbind(year, pop)
> nd<-data.frame(nd)
> nd$year<-as.factor(nd$year)
> nd$pop<-as.factor(nd$pop)

# Predict values for populations A-F for years 1-4
> getN.hat <- function(fit) {
> y <- predict(fit, newdata=nd, type="lambda")$Predicted
> z <- y * area    # area is a string of areas for each population, each year
> zz <- z$area.ha
> return(zz)
>  }

# Use parboot to estimate CI's. For final runs set nsim=200
> pred.all <- parboot(gds$yearpop._NBd, statistic=getN.hat, nsim=10)

In the calculation, the estimated density is multiplied by the surveyed area ('area'; which is different for each year and population). This script runs fine and produces realistic estimations. My problem surfaces when I set the nsim>30. R does not run very long, and churns out the following error message:

Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  7 nodes produced errors; first error: object 'nd' not found

With a larger nsim value, somehow 'nd' is not found. I am not sure what the source of this error is. Hopefully, someone in the community has experienced a similar problem or another way to get at CI's.

Thank you,
Sean Murphy
